## Today's plan

Two powerful (and tricky) toolkits:

- **Part 1: Regular expressions** (Chapter 15)
  - a compact language for describing patterns in text
- **Part 2: Dates and times** (Chapter 17)
  - creating, extracting, and computing with dates and times using **lubridate**


## Setup

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(nycflights13)
library(babynames)
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Heavy data ahead"}
`babynames` has about 1.9 million rows and the browser version of R has limited memory. If a cell crashes with a **"table index is out of bounds"** message, refresh the page and run only that cell.
:::

# Part 1: Regular expressions

## What is a regular expression?

A **regular expression** (regex or regexp) is a concise language for describing patterns in strings.

- The name sounds odd, but it's easy to see why they're useful: they pack a lot of meaning into a few characters
- They look like a cat walked across the keyboard at first
- They get easier with practice, and soon they start to make sense


## Where we're going

- **Pattern basics**: literals, metacharacters, quantifiers, classes, alternation
- **Key functions**: detect, count, replace, extract
- **Pattern details**: escaping, anchors, classes, quantifiers, precedence, grouping
- **Pattern control**: flags and fixed matches
- **Practice**: check your work, Boolean logic, patterns built by code

## Practice vectors

stringr ships with three handy character vectors:

- `fruit`: 80 fruit names
- `words`: 980 common English words
- `sentences`: 720 short sentences

```{webr}
head(fruit)
head(words)
head(sentences)
```

# Pattern basics

## `str_view()`

`str_view()` shows only the elements that match, with each match highlighted (wrapped in `<>`).

The simplest patterns are **literal characters**: they match themselves.

```{webr}
str_view(fruit, "berry")
```

## Metacharacters

Some characters have **special meaning** instead of matching themselves. Examples: `.`, `+`, `*`, `[`, `]`, `?`.

- `.` matches **any** character (except a newline)

```{webr}
str_view(c("a", "ab", "ae", "bd", "ea", "eab"), "a.")
```

```{webr}
str_view(fruit, "a...e")
```

## Quantifiers

Quantifiers control **how many times** a pattern can match:

- `?` makes the previous item optional (0 or 1 times)
- `+` repeats it 1 or more times
- `*` repeats it 0 or more times

```{webr}
# ab? matches an "a", optionally followed by a "b"
str_view(c("a", "ab", "abb"), "ab?")
# ab+ matches an "a", followed by at least one "b"
str_view(c("a", "ab", "abb"), "ab+")
# ab* matches an "a", followed by any number of "b"s
str_view(c("a", "ab", "abb"), "ab*")
```

## Character classes

Square brackets define a **character class**: match any one of the listed characters.

- `[abcd]` matches "a", "b", "c", or "d"
- `[^abcd]` matches **anything except** those (the `^` inverts it)

```{webr}
str_view(words, "[aeiou]x[aeiou]")
str_view(words, "[^aeiou]y[^aeiou]")
```

## Alternation

`|` means **or**: pick between one or more alternative patterns.

```{webr}
str_view(fruit, "apple|melon|nut")
```

```{webr}
# Repeated vowels
str_view(fruit, "aa|ee|ii|oo|uu")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Regexes are case sensitive"}
`"apple"` will not match "Apple". We'll see how to ignore case in the pattern control section.
:::

## Pattern basics: summary

| Pattern | Matches |
|---------|---------|
| `.` | any one character |
| `?` `+` `*` | 0 or 1, 1 or more, 0 or more |
| `[abc]` | any of a, b, c |
| `[^abc]` | anything except a, b, c |
| `a|b` | a or b |

# Key functions

## Four jobs for regexes

stringr has functions for the most common regex jobs:

- **Detect** matches: `str_detect()`
- **Count** matches: `str_count()`
- **Replace** matches: `str_replace()` and friends
- **Extract** pieces into columns: `separate_wider_regex()`

## `str_detect()`

`str_detect()` returns a **logical vector**: `TRUE` where the pattern matches. That means it works great inside `filter()` (and everything you learned about logical vectors applies).

```{webr}
str_detect(c("a", "b", "c"), "[aeiou]")
```

## Names containing an "x"

To avoid memory trouble, first collapse `babynames` to one row per name:

```{webr}
babynames |>
  count(name, wt = n, name = "total") |>
  filter(str_detect(name, "x")) |>
  arrange(desc(total))
```

## The proportion of names with an "x" over time

`mean()` of a logical vector gives a proportion (recall the logical vectors lecture):

```{webr}
babynames |>
  filter(year %% 5 == 0) |> 
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(prop_x = mean(str_detect(name, "x"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = prop_x)) +
  geom_line()
```


## Related: `str_subset()` and `str_which()`

- `str_subset()` returns the matching **strings**
- `str_which()` returns the **positions** of matches

```{webr}
str_subset(fruit, "berry")
str_which(fruit, "berry")
```

## `str_count()`

`str_count()` counts how many **times** the pattern matches in each string.

```{webr}
x <- c("apple", "banana", "pear")
str_count(x, "p")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Matches never overlap"}
Once a part of the string is matched, it is consumed. So `"aba"` matches only **twice** in `"abababa"`, not three times.
:::

```{webr}
str_count("abababa", "aba")
str_view("abababa", "aba")
```

## Counting vowels and consonants in names

```{webr}
babynames |>
  count(name) |>
  mutate(
    vowels = str_count(name, "[aeiou]"),
    consonants = str_count(name, "[^aeiou]")
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Look closely: Aaron has 1 vowel?"}
Regexes are case sensitive, so the capital "A" isn't in `[aeiou]`, and it counts as a **consonant**. Worse, it counts under `[^aeiou]`!
:::

## Three ways to fix the case problem

```{webr}
# 1. Add the uppercase vowels
babynames |>
  count(name) |>
  mutate(
    vowels = str_count(name, "[aeiouAEIOU]"),
    consonants = str_count(name, "[^aeiouAEIOU]")
  )
```

```{webr}
# 2. Tell the regex to ignore case
babynames |>
  count(name) |>
  mutate(
    vowels = str_count(name, regex("[aeiou]", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    consonants = str_count(name, regex("[^aeiou]", ignore_case = TRUE))
  )
```

```{webr}
# 3. Lowercase the names first
babynames |>
  count(name) |>
  mutate(
    name = str_to_lower(name),
    vowels = str_count(name, "[aeiou]"),
    consonants = str_count(name, "[^aeiou]")
  )
```

## Replacing values

- `str_replace()` replaces the **first** match
- `str_replace_all()` replaces **every** match

```{webr}
x <- c("apple", "pear", "banana")
# Replace first
str_replace(x, "[aeiou]", "-")
# Replace all
str_replace_all(x, "[aeiou]", "-")
```

## Removing values

`str_remove()` and `str_remove_all()` are shortcuts for replacing with an empty string:

```{webr}
x <- c("apple", "pear", "banana")
# Remove first
str_remove(x, "[aeiou]")
# Remove all
str_remove_all(x, "[aeiou]")
```

## Extracting variables

`separate_wider_regex()` (from tidyr) splits one column into several, using a **sequence of patterns**. Named patterns become columns; unnamed patterns are matched but dropped.

```{webr}
df <- tribble(
  ~str,
  "<Sheryl>-F_34",
  "<Kisha>-F_45",
  "<Brandon>-N_33",
  "<Sharon>-F_38",
  "<Penny>-F_58",
  "<Justin>-M_41",
)

df |>
  separate_wider_regex(
    str,
    patterns = c(
      "<",
      name = "[A-Za-z]+",
      ">-",
      gender = ".",
      "_",
      age = "[0-9]+"
    )
  )
```


## Exercise

::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"}
What baby name has the most vowels? What name has the highest proportion of vowels? (Hint: what is the denominator?)
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_1
babynames |>
  distinct(name) |>
  mutate(vowels = , length = , prop = )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_1
#| solution: true
names_vowels <- babynames |>
  distinct(name) |>
  mutate(
    vowels = str_count(name, regex("[aeiou]", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    length = str_length(name),
    prop = vowels / length
  )

names_vowels |> arrange(desc(vowels))   # most vowels
names_vowels |> arrange(desc(prop))     # highest proportion (denominator: name length)
```

## Exercise

::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"}
Replace all forward slashes in `"a/b/c/d/e"` with backslashes. What happens if you then try to replace all backslashes with forward slashes? 
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_2
x <- "a/b/c/d/e"

```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_2
#| solution: true
x <- "a/b/c/d/e"

# "\\\\" is one literal backslash in the REPLACEMENT string...
y <- str_replace_all(x, "/", "\\\\")
str_view(y)

# ...and in the PATTERN a literal backslash needs "\\\\" as well
str_replace_all(y, "\\\\", "/")
```

## Exercise

::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"}
Implement a simple version of `str_to_lower()` using `str_replace_all()`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_3
x <- "Hello WORLD"

```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rx_3
#| solution: true
x <- "Hello WORLD"
# A named vector: names are patterns, values are replacements
lookup <- setNames(letters, LETTERS)   # "A" -> "a", "B" -> "b", ...
str_replace_all(x, lookup)
```

# Pattern details


## Escaping

If `.` means "any character", how do you match a **literal dot**? You **escape** it with a backslash: `\.`

::: {.callout-warning title="Two levels of escaping"}
The regex needs `\.`, but a backslash is also special in R strings. So you write **`"\\."`** in R code: the string `\\.` becomes the regex `\.`.
:::

```{webr}
dot <- "\\."
str_view(dot)   # the regex is \.

str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "bef"), "a\\.c")
```

## Matching a literal backslash

To match a literal `\`, the regex is `\\`, which as an R string is `"\\\\"`.

```{webr}
x <- "a\\b"
str_view(x)
str_view(x, "\\\\")
```

Raw strings make this much easier to read:

```{webr}
x <- "a\\b"
str_view(x, r"{\\}")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Escape alternative"}
Instead of escaping, you can put a metacharacter inside a character class: `[.]`, `[$]`, `[|]`. These match the literal character. (The exceptions are `]`, `\`, `^`, and `-`.)
:::

```{webr}
str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "a*c", "a c"), "a[.]c")
str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "a*c", "a c"), ".[*]c")
```

## Which characters are special?

::: {.callout-important title="Metacharacters to remember"}
The full set is: `. ^ $ \ | * + ? { } [ ] ( )`

When in doubt, escape it. Escaping a character that isn't special is harmless.
:::

## Anchors

By default, a regex matches **anywhere** in the string. Anchors pin it to a position:

- `^` matches the **start** of the string
- `$` matches the **end** of the string

```{webr}
str_view(fruit, "^a")
str_view(fruit, "a$")
```

## Anchors: matching the whole string

```{webr}
str_view(fruit, "apple")
str_view(fruit, "^apple$")
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Remember the order"}
To remember which is which, try this mnemonic: if you **begin** with power (`^`), you will **end** up with money (`$`).
:::



# Fancy Numbers: Dates and times

## Why dates and times are hard

Dates and times look simple, but two facts make them tricky:

- Does every **year** have 365 days?
- Does every **day** have 24 hours?

::: {.callout-warning title="Calendar quirks"}
- **Leap years**: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, **except** centuries, unless the century is divisible by 400
- **Daylight saving time (DST)**: some days have **23** hours and some have **25**
- **Time zones**: the same moment has different clock times in different places
:::


# Creating date/times {.smaller}

## Three types

| Type | Tibble label | Meaning |
|------|--------------|---------|
| date | `<date>` | a day |
| time | `<time>` | a time within a day (uses the hms package) |
| date-time | `<dttm>` | a date plus a time: a specific instant (called **POSIXct** in base R) |

::: {.callout-important title="Use the simplest type that works"}
If you don't need the time of day, use a date. Date-times add complexity, mainly because of time zones.
:::

## Right now

```{webr}
today()
now()
```

## Creating date-times: three ways

You'll usually create them from one of these:

1. **During import**, from a file
2. **From a string**
3. **From individual components** (like year, month, day)
4. (Also) **From another date-time type**

## During import

readr automatically recognizes ISO8601 dates and date-times:

::: {.callout-note title="ISO8601"}
ISO8601 is the international standard: `YYYY-MM-DD`, largest unit first. It sorts correctly and is unambiguous.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Ambiguous dates"}
`01/02/15` can be **January 2, 2015**, **February 1, 2015**, or **February 15, 2001**, depending on the order assumed. The same text, three different dates. Always check which convention your data uses.
:::

## Format codes {.smaller}

| Code | Meaning | Example |
|------|---------|---------|
| `%Y` | 4-digit year | 2021 |
| `%y` | 2-digit year | 21 |
| `%m` | month number | 01 |
| `%B` | full month name | January |
| `%b` | abbreviated month | Jan |
| `%d` | day of month | 02 |
| `%H` | hour, 24-hour clock | 13 |
| `%I` | hour, 12-hour clock | 1 |
| `%p` | AM/PM | pm |
| `%M` | minutes | 35 |
| `%S` | seconds | 45 |
| `%Z` | time zone name | America/Chicago |
| `%z` | offset from UTC | +0800 |


## From strings: lubridate helpers

Pick the function whose letters match the **order** of the date: `y`, `m`, `d`.

```{webr}
ymd("2017-01-31")
mdy("January 31st, 2017")
dmy("31-Jan-2017")
```

- They work whatever the separators are
- They also accept unquoted numbers

```{webr}
ymd(20170131)
```

## From strings: date-times

Add `_h`, `_hm`, or `_hms` to get a date-time:

```{webr}
ymd_hms("2017-01-31 20:11:59")
mdy_hm("01/31/2017 08:01")
```

Force a time zone with `tz`:

```{webr}
ymd(20170131, tz = "UTC")
```

## From individual components

Sometimes the pieces are in separate columns, as in `flights`. Use `make_date()` or `make_datetime()`:

```{webr}
flights |>
  select(year, month, day, hour, minute) |>
  mutate(departure = make_datetime(year, month, day, hour, minute))
```

## `dep_time` stores times as HHMM

`dep_time` and friends store times as numbers like `1530`. Use `%/%` and `%%` (from last week's **Numbers** lecture!) to unpack them:

```{webr}
make_datetime_100 <- function(year, month, day, time) {
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100)
}

flights_dt <- flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |>
  mutate(
    dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time),
    arr_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, arr_time),
    sched_dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_dep_time),
    sched_arr_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_arr_time)
  ) |>
  select(origin, dest, ends_with("delay"), ends_with("time"))

flights_dt
```

```{webr}
out
is.na(out)
```

# Lecture 10 wrap-up

## What we learned

- **Regular expressions**: describe patterns, then detect, count, replace, and extract
- **Dates and times**: parse, break apart, compute with, and convert across time zones
- Both reward the same habits: **test with tricky examples**, and **be explicit** about what you mean
